endorsements.title: Considerations for the regulation of generative AI-enabled medical devices (discussion paper)
endorsements.quote: Whether an agentic GenAI-enabled device appropriately plans, sequences, and executes multi-step tasks while recognizing when a planned action sequence would exceed its intended use or safety envelope.

evidence.title: Real-Time Trust Verification for Safe Agentic Actions using TrustBench
evidence.outcome: Reduction in harmful agent actions when a pre-execution verification toolkit is used
evidence.effect: TrustBench reduced harmful actions by 87% across multiple agentic tasks. Domain-specific plugins gave 35% greater harm reduction than generic verification.
evidence.quote: Across multiple agentic tasks, TrustBench reduced harmful actions by 87%.

evidence.title: HAARF: Healthcare AI Agents Regulatory Framework - A Comprehensive Security Verification Standard for Autonomous AI Systems in Clinical Environments
evidence.effect: Baseline agent executed unauthorized tools in 56–60% of adversarial trials.
evidence.quote: In baseline conditions, the agent model executes unauthorized tools in 56–60% of adversarial trials.

evidence.title: Performance, Failures, and Oversight of a Large Language Model Agent for Clinical Data Analysis: Evaluation Study
evidence.outcome: Propagation of erroneous outputs across agent runs
evidence.effect: SAP quality did not predict code correctness, and within-mode errors propagated identically across independent repetitions.
evidence.quote: Systematic execution errors emerged: SAP quality did not predict code correctness, and within-mode errors propagated identically across independent repetitions.

evidence.title: Benchmarking the Safety of Large Language Models for Robotic Health Attendant Control
evidence.outcome: Agent LLM execution of harmful actions outside its safe envelope in simulated robot control
evidence.effect: Mean violation rate 54.4% across 72 LLMs; device manipulation and emergency delay instructions harder to refuse than overtly destructive ones.
evidence.quote: The mean violation rate across all models was 54.4\%, with more than half exceeding 50\%, and violation rates varied substantially across behavior categories, with superficially plausible instructions such as device manipulation and emergency delay proving harder to refuse than overtly destructive ones.

evidence.title: GPAgentBench-2K: Benchmarking Large Language Model Agents in Complex Clinical Action Space
evidence.outcome: Safety constraint violations by LLM agents in high-risk primary-care cases
evidence.effect: Even frontier models with the highest diagnosis accuracy violate safety constraints in over half of high-risk cases; performance degrades as action space scales.
evidence.quote: Crucially, we uncover a clinical quality-safety gap: even frontier models with the highest diagnosis accuracy violate safety constraints in over half of high-risk cases.

evidence.title: Clinical Agents Don’t Care
evidence.outcome: Agent detection of tampered patient-identity fields (erroneous inputs) rather than propagating them
evidence.effect: GPT-4.1 flagged mismatched headers as UNKNOWN in 17.4% of runs but never detected subtle faults; GPT-4.1-nano detected 4.4% of header swaps and <1% of MRN or age changes; GPT-5-chat never identified mismatches.
evidence.quote: GPT-4.1 flagged mismatched headers as UNKNOWN in 17.4% of runs but never detected subtle faults.

evidence.title: When Agentic LLMs Trust Poisoned Tools: Vulnerability of Clinical LLMs to Adversarial Guidelines
evidence.outcome: Agentic LLM rejection of adversarially modified guideline tool outputs versus authentic ones
evidence.effect: Models selected the sham in 40.6% of evaluations (59.4% accuracy); failure 54.2% to 61.7% for safety-critical changes such as removed warnings, deleted allergy information, contraindication violations and dosing errors.
evidence.quote: Models selected the sham in 40.6% of evaluations (59.4% accuracy), with the highest failure rates for safety-critical changes including removed warnings, deleted allergy information, contraindication violations and dosing errors (54.2% to 61.7% failure).

evidence.title: Clinical agents fail silently on patient identity
evidence.outcome: Agent detection of erroneous inputs and tool outputs rather than propagating them
evidence.effect: Agents usually wrote into tampered charts; GPT-5-chat never identified mismatches; other models rarely withheld writing.
evidence.quote: Clinical agents often fail to detect patient identity inconsistencies.

commentary.bottom_line: One automated benchmark reports that a pre-execution verification toolkit reduced harmful agent actions by 87%, and no study has tested the practice in a clinical setting. Seven hazard studies show that agents often take unsafe actions and pass along tampered or erroneous tool outputs, which shows why testing is needed but does not show that any detection method works in care delivery.

perspectives.view: The only test of the practice is a level 5 automated benchmark that reports no sample size or setting. It found an 87% reduction in harmful actions. A single indirect study with unknown precision supports very low certainty. The seven hazard studies show the problem is common, but they do not test whether detection reduces it.

In adversarial trials, baseline agents executed unauthorized tools 56–60% of the time. In another study, models chose sham guideline outputs in 40.6% of evaluations, and failure reached 54.2% to 61.7% when warnings or allergy data were removed. Agents rarely withheld writing into tampered charts. These rates suggest that undetected errors could reach patients.

Across 1,200,000 tool calls, GPT-4.1 flagged mismatched headers in 17.4% of runs and never detected subtle faults. GPT-4.1-nano caught under 1% of MRN or age changes. Safety violations grew as the action space scaled. Domain-specific plugins gave 35% greater harm reduction than generic verification, which suggests generic checks may miss clinical errors.

The single test of the practice reported no population or setting. Among hazard studies, only one named a population. It covered older adults in 27 agent runs in the United Kingdom, and errors propagated identically across independent repetitions. No study examined Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients.

One regulatory discussion paper describes evaluating whether an agentic device recognizes when a planned action sequence would exceed its intended use or safety envelope. The paper describes this evaluation but does not require it. The supplied evidence offers no validated test method for premarket review, because the only test is a benchmark without clinical data.

Patients cannot see an agent's tool calls, so they depend on the agent to catch tampered identity fields. In hazard benchmarks, GPT-5-chat never identified chart mismatches. Until detection is tested in care settings, patients may expect a clinician to review agent actions before those actions take effect.

commentary.research_gap: No study has tested detection of out-of-envelope action plans or erroneous tool outputs in a live or shadow clinical deployment. No study has measured the effect of detection on patient harm or reported how often detection wrongly blocks correct actions. Trials that compare domain-specific and generic verification on dosing, allergy, and patient-identity checks would address the main gaps.
commentary.underserved_note: The one test of the practice reported no population or setting. No hazard study included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations, and one hazard study included older adults. Health systems that serve these groups have no evidence on whether detection methods perform as well on their patients' records.
